title: How We Got the Old Testament
summary: From ancient scribes to the Masoretes, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the other ancient witnesses: how the Hebrew Bible was copied and preserved for more than two thousand years, where the witnesses differ, and how reliable the text is.

sections.body:
None of the original manuscripts of any biblical book survives, for the Old Testament or the New. That is not surprising; almost no ancient literary original survives from anywhere. What we have are copies, and copies of copies, and the story of how the Old Testament reached us is the story of the people who made them.

Writing was well established in the ancient Near East long before Israel existed. Israel wrote in an alphabet, a simpler system than the cuneiform of Mesopotamia or the hieroglyphs of Egypt, and inscriptions show that people in Israel and Judah could write by the ninth and eighth centuries BC. Books were written on scrolls of papyrus or of prepared animal skin, in ink, with a reed pen. The Old Testament itself describes the process. Moses writes the words of the law in a book and orders it placed beside the ark of the covenant (Deuteronomy 31:24-26); in the reign of Josiah, around 622 BC, the high priest Hilkiah finds ‘the Book of the Law’ in the temple (2 Kings 22:8); Jeremiah dictates his oracles to the scribe Baruch, and when King Jehoiakim burns the scroll column by column, Jeremiah dictates it again, and “many similar words were added to them” (Jeremiah 36:32). That last detail matters: biblical books could grow in more than one edition, and the Bible says so itself.

The oldest surviving pieces of biblical text are two tiny silver scrolls found in 1979 by the archaeologist Gabriel Barkay in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem's Old City. Dated to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, they were rolled up and worn as amulets, and they contain a form of the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, the words beginning “May the LORD bless you and keep you”. They show that this text was known, in close to its present form, while the first temple still stood.

The script changed over time. Before the exile, Hebrew was written in the old Hebrew or paleo-Hebrew script, related to Phoenician. After the exile, Jewish scribes gradually adopted the square script derived from Aramaic, which is the Hebrew alphabet used today. In this script the smallest letter is yod, which is why Jesus could speak of “a single jot” (Matthew 5:18): not even the smallest letter of the law would pass away.

For most of its history, the Hebrew Bible was written in consonants only. Hebrew is a language whose words are built mainly on consonantal roots, and a fluent reader could supply vowels from context, as an English reader can make sense of ‘th grt dcln f th rmn mpr’. A few consonants were also used to mark some long vowels, and scribes of different periods used them more or less generously, which accounts for many of the spelling differences between manuscripts.

Scribes (Hebrew soferim, ‘counters’ or ‘writers’) were trained professionals. Ezra is called “a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses” (Ezra 7:6), and the scribes who appear in the Gospels were experts in the law. Rules for copying Torah scrolls are gathered in later rabbinic literature, especially the tractate Soferim (compiled perhaps in the eighth century AD but preserving older rules): the kind of skin, the ink, the ruling of lines, the spacing between books, and the requirement that a scribe copy from a written exemplar rather than from memory. A Torah scroll with too many errors was retired, and worn-out scrolls were stored in a genizah, a storeroom for sacred texts, rather than destroyed.

Scribes also made mistakes, and textual critics, the scholars who compare manuscripts, have catalogued the common kinds. Letters that look alike in the square script (d and r, for instance, or y and w) were confused. The eye skipped from one word to the same word further down the column, leaving out what came between (called haplography), or copied a word twice (dittography). Words were divided wrongly. Some changes were deliberate: an ancient tradition records eighteen ‘corrections of the scribes’ (tiqqune soferim), places where scribes are said to have altered an expression that seemed disrespectful to God. The best-known is Genesis 18:22, where the tradition says the text once described the LORD standing before Abraham, and scribes reversed it so that Abraham stood before the LORD. Scholars debate whether all the listed places were actual changes or later explanations, but the tradition shows Jewish scribes themselves thinking honestly about their text.

Between roughly AD 500 and 1000, schools of Jewish scholars in Tiberias in Galilee, and also in Babylonia and the land of Israel more broadly, set out to fix and preserve the text in every detail. They are called Masoretes, from masorah, ‘tradition’ or ‘transmission’. They did not change the consonants they had received; they surrounded them with a system of signs that recorded how the text was read aloud in the synagogue.

They added vowel points (dots and dashes above, below, and within the letters) so that the traditional pronunciation could not be lost. They added accents, which mark stress, divide each verse into its logical parts, and guide the chanting of the text in worship; the accents function as a kind of punctuation and are often the oldest evidence for how a verse was understood. And they wrote notes in the margins, the Masorah, counting how often an unusual form occurs, noting the middle word or verse of a book, and flagging places where the written text and the traditional reading differ. In these places, called ketiv (‘what is written’) and qere (‘what is read’), the consonants on the page were left unchanged while the vowels of the word to be read aloud were attached to them. The most frequent example is the divine name YHWH, which Jews from before the time of Jesus avoided pronouncing; the Masoretes gave it the vowels of Adonai, ‘Lord’, or of Elohim, ‘God’, as a signal to say one of those instead. A misunderstanding of this convention by Christian readers in the late Middle Ages produced the hybrid form Jehovah.

The most famous Masoretic family was that of Ben Asher, working in Tiberias in the ninth and tenth centuries. The Aleppo Codex, written around 930 and pointed, according to tradition, by Aaron ben Asher himself, was regarded by the great Jewish scholar Maimonides in the twelfth century as the model text. It was kept for centuries in the main synagogue of Aleppo, Syria; when the synagogue was burned in anti-Jewish riots in 1947, about forty percent of the manuscript, including most of the Torah, was lost, and what survives is now in Jerusalem. The Leningrad Codex, copied in Cairo in 1008 or 1009 from Ben Asher exemplars, is the oldest complete manuscript of the Hebrew Bible, and it is the basis of the standard scholarly editions, including Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia (1967 to 1977) and the Biblia Hebraica Quinta now in progress, and of most modern translations. The Hebrew University Bible Project is preparing a critical edition based on the Aleppo Codex.

The first printed Hebrew Bibles appeared in the late fifteenth century. The second Rabbinic Bible, printed in Venice by Daniel Bomberg in 1524 and 1525 and edited by Jacob ben Hayyim, became the standard text for four centuries, including for the translators of the King James Version.

sections.body:
Before 1947, the oldest substantial Hebrew manuscripts of the Old Testament were the Masoretic codices of the ninth to eleventh centuries AD. The one notable exception was the Nash Papyrus, a single sheet from about the second century BC containing the Ten Commandments and the Shema, acquired in Egypt by W. L. Nash and published in 1903. Then, in the winter of 1946 to 1947, Bedouin shepherds entered a cave near Khirbet Qumran on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea and found jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade eleven caves near Qumran yielded the remains of around nine hundred manuscripts, most of them in fragments, copied between roughly the third century BC and the first century AD. Further texts came from Masada, Nahal Hever, and Wadi Murabba'at.

More than two hundred of the Qumran manuscripts are copies of books of the Hebrew Bible. Every book is represented except Esther. Psalms, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah are the most common, which fits their prominence in the New Testament as well. The most famous is the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), found in the first cave: a complete copy of all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah, about 7.3 meters (24 feet) long, usually dated to the second century BC, often placed around 125 BC. It is roughly a thousand years older than the Aleppo and Leningrad codices.

What did the scrolls show? First, that the consonantal text the Masoretes preserved was already in existence, in close to its medieval form, before the time of Jesus. The Great Isaiah Scroll differs from the Masoretic Text in many small ways, most of them spelling, grammar, and minor wording, and a second Isaiah scroll from the same cave (1QIsa-b) is closer still to the Masoretic Text. The biblical texts from Masada and Nahal Hever, from the first and early second centuries AD, are nearly identical to the Masoretic consonants. The Masoretes were guardians, not inventors.

Second, the scrolls showed that in the last centuries BC more than one form of the text of some books circulated side by side. Some Qumran manuscripts agree with the Masoretic Text, some with the Hebrew text that underlies the Septuagint, some with the Samaritan Pentateuch, and some go their own way. A Hebrew manuscript of Jeremiah (4QJer-b) matches the shorter Septuagint edition of that book, proving that the Greek translators were following a real Hebrew text and not simply abbreviating. Scholars such as Emanuel Tov (Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, first English edition 1992, revised several times since) describe this situation as textual plurality, which narrowed after AD 70 as the proto-Masoretic text became standard in rabbinic Judaism.

For translators, the scrolls have supplied readings that modern Bibles now adopt in a small number of places. The table below gives some examples a reader of this Study Bible will meet in the text or footnotes.

sections.h: The Septuagint and the Greek versions
sections.body:
The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made by Jews, beginning in Alexandria in Egypt, for Greek-speaking Jews who no longer read Hebrew well. Its name, Latin for ‘seventy’ and abbreviated LXX, comes from a legend told in the Letter of Aristeas, a Jewish writing of the second century BC: that Ptolemy II Philadelphus, king of Egypt (ruled 283 to 246 BC), asked for a translation of the Jewish law for his library, and seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, completed it in seventy-two days. The legend grew in the retelling; Philo of Alexandria and later Christian writers said the translators, working separately, produced identical versions. Historically, the Torah was probably translated in the mid-third century BC, and the other books over the following two centuries or so, by different translators of very different styles, some very literal and some quite free.

The Septuagint matters for three reasons. It was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews such as Philo and of the earliest churches outside Judea, and the New Testament writers quote it often. When Acts 7:14 says Jacob's family numbered seventy-five, it follows the Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, where the Masoretic Text has seventy; a scroll from Qumran (4QExod-b) also has seventy-five. Second, because it was translated from Hebrew manuscripts older than any Masoretic codex, it is a witness to earlier forms of the Hebrew text. In some books it preserves a different edition: its Jeremiah is about an eighth to a seventh shorter than the Masoretic Text and places the oracles against the nations in the middle of the book; its Samuel often preserves better readings; its Esther and Daniel contain additions that became the deuterocanonical portions of those books. Third, it is the Old Testament of the Eastern Orthodox churches to this day.

In the second century AD, as Christians made heavy use of the Septuagint in debate with Jews, new Jewish Greek versions were made closer to the Hebrew then current: by Aquila (around 130), a very literal version, by Symmachus, in more idiomatic Greek, and by Theodotion, whose Daniel replaced the older Greek Daniel in most Christian manuscripts. Around 240 Origen of Alexandria compiled the Hexapla, a six-column Bible setting the Hebrew, a Greek transliteration, Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion side by side, the first great work of biblical textual criticism. Only fragments survive.

Besides the Masoretic Text, the scrolls, and the Greek versions, textual critics consult several other ancient witnesses. The Samaritan Pentateuch is the Torah as preserved by the Samaritans, the community centered on Mount Gerizim near Shechem, written in a form of the old Hebrew script. Its surviving manuscripts are medieval, but its text descends from a type found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It differs from the Masoretic Text in several thousand places, most of them spelling, and it agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text in a large number of them (traditionally counted at around 1,900). A few differences are sectarian: in Deuteronomy 27:4 it has Mount Gerizim where the Masoretic Text has Mount Ebal, and it adds to the Ten Commandments a command to build an altar on Gerizim. It also preserves readings that many scholars think original, such as Cain's words to Abel in Genesis 4:8, “Let us go out to the field”, which the Masoretic Text lacks but the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac include, and which the BSB and most modern translations print.

The Targums are Aramaic translations and paraphrases made for synagogue congregations who spoke Aramaic. The Mishnah (Megillah 4:4) describes the reader of the Torah pausing after each verse so that a translator could render it into Aramaic. The official Targums, Onkelos on the Torah and Jonathan on the Prophets, were edited in the early centuries AD; others are freer and full of interpretation. The Peshitta (‘simple’ version) is the Syriac translation used by Syriac-speaking churches, its Old Testament translated from Hebrew probably in the first to third centuries AD. The Latin Vulgate is Jerome's translation from the Hebrew, made in Bethlehem between about 390 and 405, which became the Bible of the Western church for a thousand years; before it, Latin Christians used Old Latin versions translated from the Septuagint.

None of these witnesses is simply right or wrong. Each has its own history, strengths, and habits, and the textual critic weighs them one reading at a time.

sections.h: How reliable is the Old Testament text?
sections.body:
Textual criticism of the Old Testament works by comparing the witnesses, reading by reading, and asking which reading best explains how the others arose. Scholars prefer, other things being equal, the reading that would have been hardest for a scribe to invent (since scribes tended to smooth difficulties), the reading that explains the origin of the alternatives, and the reading supported by independent witnesses. They also ask whether a difference comes from a copying slip or from a different edition of a book, since some books, like Jeremiah and Samuel, circulated in more than one literary form. Accessible introductions include Paul Wegner's A Student's Guide to Textual Criticism of the Bible (2006) and Emanuel Tov's standard handbook.

The results can be stated fairly. The consonantal text of the Hebrew Bible that underlies English Old Testaments was transmitted with remarkable care for well over a thousand years, as the comparison between the Dead Sea Scrolls and the medieval codices shows. Most differences among the witnesses are small: spelling, word order, a conjunction, a single word. A modest number of passages have differences that affect meaning, like those in the table above, and English Bibles note many of them in footnotes. In a few books, especially Jeremiah, Samuel, Esther, and Daniel, the Septuagint represents a different edition, and scholars debate how those editions relate to one another and which form should be translated.

Scholars also differ in method. Most standard translations translate the Masoretic Text and depart from it only where another witness is clearly better, as the BSB does in the passages noted above. Some scholars, including Ronald Hendel and the project called The Hebrew Bible: A Critical Edition, are building eclectic texts that reconstruct the earliest recoverable form book by book. Others, especially in Jewish scholarship, value the Masoretic Text as the received text of a living community and study the other witnesses as parts of its history rather than as corrections to it. Christian traditions add their own question: the Orthodox read the Septuagint as their Old Testament, and Catholics and Protestants have long consulted it where the Hebrew is obscure.

What a reader of this Study Bible can take from all this is simple. When the notes mention the Masoretic Text, the Dead Sea Scrolls, or the Septuagint, they are describing real witnesses, handled in the open, with their differences stated. The Old Testament we read is not a medieval invention; it is the text the Masoretes received from scribes who were already copying it in the age of the Maccabees, and in its substance the text Jesus and the apostles read. As Isaiah put it of the word of God, in a verse the Great Isaiah Scroll preserves as clearly as any modern Bible: “the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8).
